items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🧬 Asteroid Ryugu now contains the full alphabet of DNA and RNA.

Scientists have detected all five canonical nucleobases in samples returned from Ryugu by Japan’s Hayabusa2 mission.

These are adenine, guanine, cytosine, thymine and uracil, the molecular letters used by life on Earth to build DNA and RNA.

This does not mean life existed on Ryugu.

It means that some of the key ingredients used by genetic molecules can form in space and survive inside ancient asteroid material.

That makes Ryugu incredibly valuable.

Unlike meteorites that fall through Earth’s atmosphere and touch soil, Ryugu’s samples were collected directly from the asteroid and sealed for return to Earth.

That helps scientists study asteroid chemistry with far less contamination.

The discovery also matches what researchers have found in samples from asteroid Bennu, where all five nucleobases were detected too.

Together, Ryugu and Bennu suggest that the chemistry behind DNA and RNA was not rare in the early Solar System.

Long before life began on Earth, asteroids may have been carrying the molecular letters life would later use to write its genetic code.

The rocks were not alive.

But they may have delivered part of life’s alphabet.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Koga et al., “A complete set of canonical nucleobases in the carbonaceous asteroid (162173) Ryugu”, Nature Astronomy (2026)

items.text:
LOS ANGELES EARTHQUAKE UPDATE‼️over the weekend, 107 earthquakes were recorded across two areas of Southern California! 101 earthquakes near Lennox, Inglewood and Hawthorne. This activity is near the Newport-Inglewood Fault Zone. The strongest earthquake in this sequence was a magnitude 2.7 near Lennox early Saturday morning. And 6 earthquakes approximately 16 miles east-southeast of Avalon. This activity is near the offshore San Pedro Basin fault system. The strongest was a magnitude 3.3 early Saturday morning, preceded two minutes earlier by a magnitude 3.0.

Many people may not have felt these earthquakes because most were extremely small. Many of the Lennox-area earthquakes also originated roughly 10-15 miles underground, while the Avalon sequence occurred offshore and several miles beneath the seafloor. Shaking from small, deep or offshore earthquakes often weakens considerably before reaching populated areas.

These appear to be two separate sequences. Their proximity to mapped faults does not confirm that those specific faults produced the earthquakes, and swarms do not necessarily mean a larger earthquake is coming. The numbers and preliminary magnitudes may change as seismic data are reviewed‼️

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🧲 It’s official: physicists have directly imaged a strange third class of magnetic order.

For a long time, scientists mostly sorted ordered magnets into two major families.

Ferromagnets are the familiar kind. Their tiny magnetic moments line up in the same direction, creating an overall magnetic field.

Antiferromagnets are different. Their moments point in opposite directions, cancelling each other out so the material has no net magnetization.

Now, researchers have confirmed a third class called altermagnetism.

In an altermagnet, the magnetic moments also point in opposite directions. But the atomic environment around each moment is rotated in a special way.

That small geometric twist changes everything.

It gives the material some of the speed and stability of an antiferromagnet, while also allowing useful electronic effects normally associated with ferromagnets.

Using X-ray microscopy, scientists imaged altermagnetic domains inside manganese telluride, a material once treated as a simple antiferromagnet.

They also showed that these domains can be controlled in microscopic devices.

That matters because altermagnets could help build faster, denser and more energy-efficient memory and spintronic technologies.

They may even provide new clues in the physics of superconductivity.

A hidden form of magnetism has finally stepped into view.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Amin et al., “Nanoscale imaging and control of altermagnetism in MnTe”, Nature (2024)

A CLOUD CREATED BY FIRE 🔥

Check this out from yesterday’s fire in Western Oklahoma. The intense heat generated enough lift to produce these pyrocumulus clouds directly above the smoke plume.

They form when extremely hot air from a wildfire rapidly rises, cools and condenses. If the updraft becomes strong enough, these clouds can grow significantly and, in extreme cases, develop into pyrocumulonimbus clouds capable of producing lightning and even their own weather.

Pretty incredible example of just how much energy a large fire can put into the atmosphere.

OpenAI says an internal AI system has produced a proof for the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the famous Millennium Prize Problems.

The question asks whether smooth fluid motion can suddenly break down and form a singularity.

In OpenAI’s claimed solution, a fluid starts smoothly from rest, keeps finite energy, but develops unbounded velocity in finite time.

That would be historic.

But the scale of the effort is just as striking.

OpenAI says the Navier-Stokes run used about 10,000 concurrent AI agents working for 88 hours.

Those agents exchanged 2.7 million messages and generated around 130 billion output tokens.

Across all the major problems OpenAI tested, the system used 4.9 million messages and about 300 billion output tokens.

Then GPT-6 Astra spent another 17 hours formalizing and checking the proof in Lean.

In other words, this was not one AI calmly thinking like a lone mathematician.

It was a huge industrial swarm of machines attacking a frontier problem with computing power that almost no academic group could match.

That is where the controversy begins.

NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge had been working on closely related fluid equations and had used OpenAI tools during their research.

Buckmaster worried that private, unfinished work shared inside Codex could somehow have helped OpenAI’s system.

OpenAI denies this and says Buckmaster’s Codex prompts could not have influenced the result.

For now, the proof still needs mathematical scrutiny.

But the bigger question is already here.

When AI companies can provide the tools, hear that researchers are close, and then throw millions of machine hours at the same problem, science enters a very different world.

📄 TECHNICAL PAPER
📌 OpenAI, “Finite Time Blowup for Navier-Stokes”, OpenAI (2026)

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🌊 The detectors had only been switched on for a few days. Scientists were still running tests, fine-tuning the equipment, not officially looking for anything yet. Then, at a moment when nobody was really watching, a signal rolled in from a collision that had happened 1.3 billion years ago. The universe didn't wait for them to be ready.

On September 14, 2015, the two LIGO observatories, one in Washington state and one in Louisiana, picked up the first gravitational waves ever directly detected. The signal came from two black holes, roughly 36 and 29 times the mass of our Sun, spiraling together and merging into one. In the final fraction of a second, they released more energy than all the stars in the observable universe combined, all of it as ripples in space-time itself.

Those ripples had been traveling for 1.3 billion years before they washed over Earth and stretched the LIGO detectors by a fraction of the width of a proton. The whole event, captured as a rising "chirp," lasted about two-tenths of a second.

The signal was so clean that some team members initially suspected it was a fake test injection. It wasn't. It was real. Einstein had predicted this exactly a century earlier, and almost nobody thought we'd ever actually catch one.

Our trip to Glacier National Park with our dear friends Matt and Carrie Harris was amazing and just what Cindy and I needed.

It’s been seven weeks since Mom passed. We’re still adjusting to a new normal, and some days the emotional and physical exhaustion catches up with me. I’m not overwhelmed by grief every moment, but I rarely sleep through the night. I wake up three or four times, often without a dream or even a thought about Mom. I don’t know whether that’s part of grieving, me turning 60 in December or just a coincidence. Maybe time will tell.

This was our first big trip since she passed, and I’ll be honest, I sometimes felt guilty even planning it. Part of me wondered whether enjoying myself meant I wasn’t honoring her enough, or that I was moving on too quickly.

After a lot of prayer and reflection, I now know better. I will never “get over” losing Mom. But she wouldn’t want us to stop living, either. Because her health made travel difficult, she loved experiencing adventures through us. She always wanted pictures, and she couldn’t wait to hear every story when we got home. I believe she had an even better view of this trip from heaven.

Glacier did our souls good. We thought of Mom often, and out there in God’s country, we felt close to her. I’ll always cherish that.

Life keeps moving. We’ll take the trips, make the memories, and carry Mom’s love with us wherever we go. I can’t think of a better way to honor her.

TROPICS | SEPT 14, 2026 4 AM | NHC has increased the chance of a system developing in the Atlantic NE of the islands to 30% over the next 7 days. 

A weak wave will travel into a more favorable location for development this week & some tropical system formation here is possible later in the week.

There is a HUGE difference among the models with this system & it's a rather unusual one. The difference here is not EURO vs GFS; it's traditional vs AI. The traditional physics-based models are not doing much with a system in this region. They really don't have much, if anything, forming here. 

On the other hand, the AI models are going CRAZY, calling for tropical storm & maybe even hurricane development. The next name on the list is Fay.

The AI models have been a lot more bullish with systems this year overall. The AI ensembles show MANY more potential storm tracks vs. the traditional models. The indicators for this system from the AI models are the strongest we've seen in any system so far this year. 

The threat to the U.S. from this is VERY low. There will be a couple of cold fronts coming off the U.S. East Coast in the next 5-10 days. These fronts would keep this system out to sea; a fish storm. All the AI models turn this system north & northeast AWAY from the U.S. East Coast. 

For Florida, this storm would form too far north to be a threat.  

I'll keep you updated.

items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE
items.text:
BAD DAY IN WEATHER HISTORY

37 years ago today, Hurricane Hugo was intensifying and became a major hurricane (category 3) with 115 mph winds as it approached the Lesser Antilles. 18 hours later, it would become a category 5 with winds of 160 mph.

7 years ago, Hurricane Florence came ashore in southeast North Carolina then crawled across South Carolina dumping nearly 2 feet of rain. That sent rivers to levels that shattered records set by Hurricane Matthew in 2016.

Hugo was an example of the sheer destructive power of wind and surge.

Florence was an example of how catastrophic rain can be. Because of how painstakingly slow Hurricane Florence moved, unprecedented rainfall produced catastrophic flooding, especially on our rivers. Record river crests set by Matthew in 2016 were shattered by inches to over 3 ft with Hurricane Florence.

And to think, it was "just a tropical storm" that moved through our area. We had no hurricane-force winds.

Lesson here. The amount of rainfall from a tropical system isn't proportional to the strength of the system, it's proportional to the speed of the system. As mentioned, Florence was a tropical storm when it moved through our area yet it dumped nearly 24" of rain in spots. It was literally crawling at 3 mph. Hurricane Hugo was a category 4 hurricane that barreled across the Carolinas at over 25 mph. It only produced 2-8" of rain across the state.

items.text:
Tinnitus is the perception of ringing, buzzing, clicking, or hissing when no external sound is present.

For many people, the problem is not only in the ears. The brain may become stuck treating phantom sound as important instead of filtering it into the background.

A new review suggests psilocybin, the psychedelic compound in magic mushrooms, could affect some of the same brain systems involved in tinnitus.

These include serotonin signaling, glutamate, GABA, and brain plasticity — the brain’s ability to reshape its connections.

A mouse study also suggests psilocybin can change how the brain filters repeated sounds.

But no clinical trial has shown that psilocybin safely treats tinnitus in humans.

For now, this is a research direction, not a therapy.

📃 REVIEW PAPER
📌 Lu et al., “Current status and future prospects of research on psilocybin's regulation of neurotransmitters and their receptors related to the pathogenesis of tinnitus”, Hearing Research (2026)

TROPICS | SEPT 13, 2026 | The NHC is watching a disorganized area of clouds in the central Atlantic. This system is in an area of high shear & development is not likely over the next couple of days. 

After that, by about mid-week, it will move farther WNW, where shear is less & conditions are a bit more conducive to some slow development. 

Though the regular models show nothing coming out of this, both the EURO AI & Google DeepMind do have a few of their ensembles developing into an actual system. Overall, actually, the chances of these models of development later in the week are better than they've been with previous systems these models have tracked this season. 

Though the ensemble tracks are all over the place, none of the models bring the system toward the U.S. East Coast. They all turn the system north or away. 

For Florida, either way, this would not be an issue. By the time this gets into an area favorable for development, it would be at our latitude or farther north. A track west from that location is unlikely, especially for a strengthening system which would be pulled more north. 

Still, a tropical storm here is possible in the next 4-7 days. The next name on the list is Fay.

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
♾️ Webb has spotted a distant galaxy shaped like an infinity symbol, and something strange is happening at its center.

The object is called the Infinity Galaxy, and it lies about 8.3 billion light-years away.

It appears to be the aftermath of a head-on collision between two disk galaxies.

Each galaxy has a compact red nucleus surrounded by a ring of stars and gas, giving the whole system the shape of a sideways 8.

But the real surprise is not the shape.

Using JWST, Chandra, Keck and the Very Large Array, astronomers found an actively feeding supermassive black hole between the two galactic nuclei.

That is not where supermassive black holes are usually found.

They normally sit at the centers of galaxies.

Here, the black hole appears embedded in a vast cloud of shocked and compressed gas created by the collision.

One possibility is that the black hole formed right there, through direct collapse, when a dense gas cloud collapsed under its own gravity instead of first making stars.

If confirmed, this could be one of the clearest glimpses yet of a newborn supermassive black hole.

A cosmic collision may have created a black hole seed in real time.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 van Dokkum et al., “The ∞ Galaxy: A Candidate Direct-Collapse Supermassive Black Hole Between Two Massive, Ringed Nuclei”, The Astrophysical Journal Letters (2025)

ACTIVE MONSOON PATTERN FOR SOUTHWEST THIS UPCOMING WEEK🌧️🌵confidence continues to increase that a more active and wetter weather pattern will develop across parts of Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado, Utah and far West Texas this upcoming week and next weekend! 

The overall setup supports this wetter signal. The subtropical ridge that has dominated much of the Southwest is shifting east while a trough develops across the western U.S. This places much of the region beneath persistent south-to-southwest flow capable of transporting deeper subtropical/monsoonal moisture northward. This is reflected in the Climate Prediction Center’s latest 6-10 day precipitation outlook, which favors above-normal precipitation across the region. 

🌵ARIZONA: moisture is already increasing, and abundant moisture is expected to remain across central and eastern Arizona well into next week. Precipitable water values could run around 150-180% of normal, supporting repeated opportunities for thunderstorms. Monday through Tuesday currently appears particularly favorable, although the exact timing of the most active periods remains uncertain. Heavy rainfall and localized flash flooding could become concerns where stronger storms develop.

🌧️NEW MEXICO: the signal is even more impressive. A surge of rich monsoon moisture is expected beginning Sunday and continuing through much of next week as Arizona and New Mexico become positioned within a favorable moisture-convergence zone. Precipitable water values may reach or exceed the 95th percentile, supporting repeated rounds of showers and thunderstorms and an increasing heavy-rain-flash-flood threat. The overall pattern increasingly favors some much-needed widespread rainfall.

⛈️COLORADO: monsoonal moisture will also be drawn northward into Colorado. Storm chances increase Sunday before moist southwesterly flow and stronger forcing bring considerably better precipitation chances Monday and Tuesday. Monsoonal moisture may remain in place through late next week, supporting daily shower and thunderstorm chances and a cooler, wetter pattern.

🌵FAR WEST TEXAS: the El Paso region should also increasingly become involved as deeper moisture spreads north. The broader pattern favors better opportunities for thunderstorms and locally heavy rainfall as we head deeper into next week.

🌵EASTERN UTAH: this area increasingly looks like part of the wetter pattern. Moist southwest flow is expected to become established, with atmospheric moisture potentially reaching 150-200% of normal across much of the region. That should support increasing shower and thunderstorm coverage, including opportunities for locally moderate to heavy rainfall. Southeast Utah appears particularly favored for monsoonal moisture.

The important takeaway is not that it will rain everywhere every day. There will still be considerable day-to-day variability in thunderstorm coverage. But the large-scale environment is becoming substantially more favorable for repeated monsoonal moisture surges and thunderstorms🌧️⛈️

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text:
DOES THIS PATTERN LOOK LIKE EL NIÑO❓IT DOES🌧️⛈️take a look at the precipitation pattern expected across the Lower-48 over the next couple of weeks. There are definitely some characteristics that resemble the type of pattern we often associate with El Niño.

The Climate Prediction Center’s 6-10 day outlook, covering September 17-21, favors above-normal precipitation across a large part of the Southwest, Rockies and Southern Plains. Arizona, New Mexico, Utah, Colorado, Nevada, southern California, Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas are among the areas leaning wetter than normal. This is likely due to a tropical moisture transport responsible for the wetter signal across much of the West with the highest probabilities  centered over the Southwest and nearby areas. There is also a wetter signal extending from parts of the Mississippi and Ohio valleys toward the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast, while the Northern Plains and Upper Midwest lean drier. The Pacific Northwest, particularly Washington also initially leans drier. A similar signal continues with the 8-14 day outlook for September 19-25.

Does that mean every part of this pattern is being caused by El Niño? No! Individual troughs, ridges, tropical systems and shorter-term atmospheric variability are still driving the day-to-day weather. But the broader setup is interesting as we have a strengthening El Niño in the tropical Pacific, an active Eastern and Central Pacific, and an increasingly noticeable pipeline of tropical-subtropical moisture into parts of the western and southern United States. That combination - enhanced southern-tier-Pacific moisture with an increasingly active storm track across portions of the southern and western U.S. - certainly has an El Niño flavor to it. Also, remember, we're only in September. The classic El Niño influence on the U.S. becomes considerably more important as we move toward late fall and winter🌧️⛈️

WE HAD A CLOSE ENCOUNTER WITH A GRIZZLY BEAR! 🐻

Matt & Carrie Harris and Cindy & I were hiking the Highline Trail in Glacier National Park on Saturday when we spotted a grizzly in the distance, on the trail and heading our way. I took the first zoomed-in video while he was still about 200 yards away.

If you’ve hiked the Highline, you know some stretches are so narrow there’s nowhere to step aside. So we backtracked a bit then climbed the rocks to higher a perch above the trail to give him plenty of room to pass. In the second video, Matt was still climbing higher as the bear walked by just below us!

We stood quietly together with bear spray in hand, hoping he’d keep going rather than come up toward us. Thankfully, he went on his merry way. We’re grateful everyone is safe, and we have one wild story to tell!

That was our first encounter with a grizzly bear. Honestly, it was a heart-pounding moment!

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text:
DOES THIS PATTERN LOOK A LITTLE LIKE EL NIÑO? IT DOES🌧️take a look at the precipitation pattern expected across the Lower-48 over the next couple of weeks. There are definitely some characteristics that resemble the type of pattern we often associate with El Niño.

The Climate Prediction Center’s 6-10 day outlook, covering September 17-21, favors above-normal precipitation across a large part of the Southwest, Rockies and Southern Plains. Arizona, New Mexico, Utah, Colorado, Nevada, southern California, Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas are among the areas leaning wetter than normal. This is likely due to a tropical moisture transport responsible for the wetter signal across much of the West with the highest probabilities  centered over the Southwest and nearby areas. There is also a wetter signal extending from parts of the Mississippi and Ohio valleys toward the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast, while the Northern Plains and Upper Midwest lean drier. The Pacific Northwest, particularly Washington also initially leans drier. A similar signal continues with the 8-14 day outlook for September 19-25.

Does that mean every part of this pattern is being caused by El Niño? No! Individual troughs, ridges, tropical systems and shorter-term atmospheric variability are still driving the day-to-day weather. But the broader setup is interesting as we have a strengthening El Niño in the tropical Pacific, an active Eastern and Central Pacific, and an increasingly noticeable pipeline of tropical-subtropical moisture into parts of the western and southern United States. That combination - enhanced southern-tier-Pacific moisture with an increasingly active storm track across portions of the southern and western U.S. - certainly has an El Niño flavor to it. Also, remember, we're only in September. The classic El Niño influence on the U.S. becomes considerably more important as we move toward late fall and winter🌧️

🇺🇸 25 years later, we must never forget.

Yesterday at the 9/11 Commemoration at OCC Road House, I had the privilege of hearing Greg Mertz, a retired United States Secret Service agent, share his remarkable story from September 11, 2001.

Greg was with President George W. Bush in Florida that morning and walked us through the events almost minute by minute — the uncertainty, the split-second decisions, and the responsibility of protecting the President as our country came under attack.

But his service didn’t end there. Shortly afterward, Greg was sent to Ground Zero, where he spent almost two weeks assisting with the heartbreaking search and recovery effort.

Listening to him describe what he witnessed, the people he encountered, and the weight carried by everyone working at Ground Zero was incredibly moving. You could hear the emotion in his voice even 25 years later.

Greg, thank you for your service to our country, for what you did on that terrible day and in the days that followed, and for continuing to share your story so future generations understand what happened and why we must never forget.

I’m also grateful that several members of our team were there with me to share in such a meaningful day of remembrance and reflection.

We honor the innocent lives we lost, the heroes who ran toward danger, and all those whose lives were forever changed by September 11.

🇺🇸 Never Forget.

items.author: JeffBerardelli
items.text:
The Ocean’s En Fuego! 
15% of the oceans are record warm right now. Double the record of 7.3% set back in 2023 for Mid Sept. 
This heat will impact Earth’s weather patterns through spring. For now it means active Pacific hurricanes, inactive Atlantic. But the bigger impact comes in late fall & winter, with a supercharged Pacific subtropical jet stream across the southern US. It will bring heavy rain storms to California, and the Southeast, Gulf Coast, and #Florida, with the likelihood of enhanced severe weather outbreaks as well. 
(data NOAA OISST) #elnino
